title: Identity Governance
summary: Identity governance is the set of processes and controls that decide who should hold which access, prove that the access remains appropriate, and remove it when the reason for it disappears. It covers joiner, mover and leaver workflows, access request and approval routing, role and entitlement modelling, periodic access reviews, separation-of-duties rules, privileged access management integration, and the evidence trail an auditor expects. It is distinct from authentication and from single sign-on: those answer who you are and whether you may sign in now, while governance answers whether you should still hold each entitlement, and whether someone accountable agreed. The mistake is running reviews as a rubber stamp where a manager approves hundreds of rows without usage context, which produces signed evidence and a measurable reduction in nothing. Governance reduces standing privilege only when reviews carry real data, reviewers can say no, and removals actually reach the target systems.

beginner.definition: Identity governance is the way a company decides who may use which systems. It gives people access when they join. It changes that access when they move to a new job. It removes access when they leave. It also asks managers to check that old access is still needed. The goal is simple, nobody keeps access they no longer require.
beginner.whyItMatters: Accounts and permissions pile up over the years. Someone changes team but keeps access to the old system. A contractor leaves but the account stays open. Every leftover permission is a door an attacker can walk through. Governance finds those doors and closes them. It also gives auditors proof that the company checks its own access.
howItWorks: A new person joins, and a defined process grants the access for that role.
Requests for extra access go to a system owner, who approves or refuses.
When the person changes role, old access is reviewed and then reduced.
When the person leaves, every account is disabled on the same day.
Managers review a list of access at set times and confirm or remove it.
The system stores who approved what, so each decision can be proved later.
beginner.example: Think of a large office building where each door needs a key card. When you join, the front desk gives you a card for the doors your job needs. When you move to another floor, some doors are removed from your card and others are added. When you leave, the card stops working that same day. Every few months the security desk prints the list and each manager checks it. Identity governance is that desk and that list for computer accounts.
takeaways: Grant access at join, review it at role change and remove it at departure.
A review only helps when the reviewer has the context to answer no.
Keep the approval records, because they are the evidence auditors ask for.

objectives: Explain what identity governance covers and how it differs from authentication.
Describe the joiner, mover and leaver process for a realistic organisation.
Explain the purpose of access reviews, role modelling and separation-of-duties rules.
Identify the evidence an auditor expects from a governance programme.
Recognise a rubber-stamp review and describe how to make it meaningful.
